parts.text: These organisations achieve high reliability because their baseline assumption is that they are not safe. They remain attentive to

of bigger problems, do not automatically dismiss anomalies, learn from near misses and failures and build redundancy – for example, backing up offline systems and providing kill switches.

They routinely rehearse failure, establish operational processes, adhere to regulation for safety and

, comply with professional standards and certification schemes and have independent oversight. High reliability organisations give experts the authority to challenge decisions. They continuously learn from their performance.

This provides a very different way of thinking about AI

. Instead of asking simply, “how do we regulate AI?” we should ask: “what would a high-reliability organisation look like if AI was embedded throughout it?”

This suggests that AI safety cannot be reduced to a model passing a one-off

test before deployment. It must span different organisations and transcend international boundaries.

AI assurance

This is where the current political conversation about AI regulation risks being too narrow. Governments need to understand what frontier

are developing. But government cannot realistically sit permanently inside every AI company and inspect every model.

Nor can legislation anticipate every technical configuration that AI will take. The UK government recognises it must cultivate trustworthiness in AI through assurance.
Assurance asks whether there is

evidence that a system is behaving within defined boundaries, whether those boundaries are appropriate, whether risks are being monitored and whether someone is accountable when they are breached.

The aircraft industry has

standards, certification regimes, professional qualifications, independent inspection, incident reporting and regulatory oversight.

Nuclear power operates within an elaborate ecosystem of safety engineering and
regulatory assurance. Financial institutions and medicine both have

systems of assurance.

AI is becoming increasingly consequential, yet its assurance infrastructure remains
comparatively immature. This is particularly striking given the speed at which frontier systems are developing. The

challenge is not simply to produce more AI regulation, but to create the professional safety culture that makes regulation meaningful.

A potential new multinational treaty on the safe and regulated development of superintelligence would frame AI safety as a rapidly evolving global
challenge. At the same time, it
creates a once-in-a-generation opportunity for the UK to help shape the emerging architecture of AI governance.
